Advantages of the RTD

Four jobs a measured RTD does

Diagnose

Reactor illness: dead volume, bypass, recirculation.

Measure the deviation

How far the flow is from plug flow or mixed flow.

Design

Predict conversion for a microfluid or a macrofluid.

Phase hold-up

Mean residence time of each phase, e.g. liquid and gas in a trickle bed.

Limit: one RTD can belong to many different internal flows.

Reactor behaviour evaluation

The RTD is one of four things that decide conversion

Can two systems with the same RTD give a different conversion? Yes.
  • What else matters, then?
  • Can the RTD predict conversion without a model?
  • How wide is the range of answers for one RTD?
  1. Kineticsrate law and order $n$
  2. RTDhow long each element stays
  3. Micro or macro(segregation model)
  4. Earliness of mixingwhere elements meet

segregation, animated

Microfluid and macrofluid

  • Microfluid: molecules lose identity; one uniform concentration.
  • Macrofluid: each clump keeps its own concentration, like a small batch reactor.
Same RTD in both tanks: inside, the fluid may behave as a microfluid or a macrofluid.

Shade = age since entry.

Same tank, same RTD: the microfluid blends ages molecule by molecule; the macrofluid keeps each age in its packet.

Two-phase contacting

In two phases, the contactor decides which is which

  • A stream of solids always behaves as a macrofluid.
  • Gas and liquid can each be either — the dispersed phase is the macrofluid.

Two-phase reactors are treated in later chapters; here we only name the behaviour.

Factor 3 · earliness of mixing

Where along the vessel do elements mix?

All three can share the same RTD: the tracer cannot see where elements mix inside.
For a single flowing fluid this factor usually has little effect on the overall behaviour.

Reactor modelling with RTD

The RTD tells how long, not who mixed with whom

First order: the RTD is enough

The rate is linear in $C_A$: mixing before or after reacting gives the same result.

$$\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_i=e^{-kt_i}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\sum_i e^{-kt_i}\,\mathbf E_i\,\Delta t_i$$

Mixed-flow E turns the sum into $1/(1+k\bar t)$; any other E gives its own value.

Other orders: the RTD gives bounds

The rate depends on local concentration, so micro or macro, early or late mixing all matter.

The answer lies between earliest mixing (microfluid) and latest mixing (segregation integral).

Exception: plug flow and batch, where every element has the same age.

Put the pieces together: one decision tree for the design.

Micromixing and macromixing

Micromixing picks the route; macromixing sets the RTD

$t_r$
reaction time, the time the reaction needs to proceed
s
$t_{mix}$
micromixing time: molecules from different clumps meet; not the vessel’s flow pattern
s

Lecture 13-1

What section 13-1 settled

  • Transport effects, non-ideal flow among them, enter at the pilot and industrial scales; the RTD measures the flow part.
  • Conversion depends on kinetics and three contacting factors: RTD, micro or macro (segregation model), earliness of mixing.
  • $t_{mix}\ll t_r$: microfluid; $t_{mix}\gg t_r$: macrofluid, each clump a batch reactor.
  • One RTD can hide either behaviour: the tracer cannot see micromixing or where elements mix.
  • First order: the RTD alone gives conversion. Other orders: the RTD gives bounds, earliest to latest mixing.
  • Microfluid: flow model + balance, $D/uL$ or $N$ from $\mathbf E$. Macrofluid: segregation integral over $\mathbf E$.

13.1 · problem statement · read first

Conversion in a reactor with ideal flow

A liquid-phase reaction $\text{A}+\text{B}\to\text{C}+\text{D}$ has the apparent rate expression $r_1=kC_A$ with $k=0.307\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

inlet volumetric flow rate$v=200$ L/min
volume of reactor$V=3\ \text{m}^3=3000$ L
feed of A$F_{A0}=200$ mol/min

Find the conversion of A if the reactor is (a) an ideal mixed-flow reactor, (b) an ideal plug-flow reactor.

13.1 · solution, step 1

Feed concentration and space time first

Definitions$C_{A0}=\dfrac{F_{A0}}{v},\qquad \tau=\dfrac{V}{v}$
$$C_{A0}=\frac{F_{A0}}{v}=\frac{200\ \text{mol/min}}{200\ \text{L/min}}=1\ \text{mol/L}$$
concentration = molar flow over volumetric flow
$$\tau=\bar t=\frac{V}{v}=\frac{3000\ \text{L}}{200\ \text{L/min}}=15\ \text{min}\qquad k\tau=0.307\times15=4.605$$
liquid, $\varepsilon_A=0$, so space time equals mean residence time

First order: $X_A$ depends on $k\tau$ only; $V$, $v$ and $C_{A0}$ do not appear separately.

13.1 · solution, step 2 · (a) mixed flow

Mixed flow: $X_A=0.821$

Mixed-flow balance$F_{A0}-F_A=(-r_A)V$
$$\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\frac{1}{1+k\tau}=\frac{1}{5.605}=0.178$$
first-order mixed-flow result, $k\tau=4.605$

$X_A=1-0.178=$ 0.821

v=200 //L/min V=3000 //L k= 0.307 //min^-1 FA0=200 //mol/min CA0=FA0/v t=V/v //Mixed flow FA-FA0=-r1*V r1=k*CA CA=FA/v x=(FA0-FA)/FA0 { results: FA = 35.68, CA = 0.1784, x = 0.8216 }

Plug flow: $X_A=0.990$

Plug-flow balance$\dfrac{dF_A}{dV}=-(-r_A)$
$$\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=e^{-k\tau}=e^{-4.605}=0.0100$$

Plug flow · the mole balance

Plug flow: $u\,dC_A/dl=-kC_A^{\,n}$ step 2 of 2

Step 1$\dfrac{v}{S}\dfrac{dC_A}{dl}=-(-r_A)$
$$u\frac{dC_A}{dl}=-kC_A^{\,n}$$
$u=v/S$; power-law rate $-r_A=kC_A^{\,n}$
$$\frac{dC_A}{dz}=-k\tau\,C_A^{\,n},\qquad z=\frac{l}{L},\ \ \tau=\frac{L}{u},\qquad z=0:\ C_A=C_{A0}$$
multiply by $L/u$; the inlet sees the feed

The balance step 1 of 2

Steady state: out − in, plus reaction, equals zero

bulk flow: $\ C\,uS$
mol/s carried in at $l$, out at $l+\Delta l$
dispersion: $\ -DS\,\dfrac{dC}{dl}$
Fick-like flux down the gradient
reaction: $\ (-r_A)\,S\,\Delta l=kC^nS\,\Delta l$
consumed inside the slice
$D\dfrac{d^2C}{dl^2}-u\dfrac{dC}{dl}-kC^n=0$
divide by $S\Delta l$, let $\Delta l\to0$

The balance step 2 of 2

Three groups decide the conversion

$$\underbrace{\color{#C00000}\boxed{\frac{D}{uL}\frac{d^2C}{dz^2}}}_{\text{new: dispersion}}\;\underbrace{-\frac{dC}{dz}-k\tau\,C^n}_{\text{plug flow}}=0,\qquad z=\frac{l}{L}$$
$z=0:\ \ uC_0=uC(0^+)-D\dfrac{dC}{dl}\Big|_{0^+}$
flux from the feed = convection + dispersion just inside the inlet
$C_0=C(0^+)\;{\color{#C00000}\boxed{-\dfrac{D}{uL}\dfrac{dC}{dz}}}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad C(0^+)=C_0+\dfrac{D}{uL}\dfrac{dC}{dz}<C_0$
divide by $u$, $l=zL$; boxed term is new; $dC/dz<0$, so $C$ starts below $C_0$
$z=1:\ \dfrac{dC}{dz}=0$
closed outlet; groups $k\tau C_0^{\,n-1}$, $D/uL$, $n$ set $C$

First order, exactly

First order has an exact answer

$$\frac{C}{C_0}=\frac{4a\,\exp\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{uL}{D}\right)}{(1+a)^2\exp\!\left(\dfrac{a}{2}\dfrac{uL}{D}\right)-(1-a)^2\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{a}{2}\dfrac{uL}{D}\right)}$$
$$a=\sqrt{1+4k\tau\,(D/uL)}$$

Wehner & Wilhelm (1956), Levenspiel Eq. 19, for any entrance and exit conditions. Plotted on the chart that follows.

Small deviations

Small $D/uL$: expand the exponentials

Expand this for small $D/uL$$a=\sqrt{1+4k\tau\,(D/uL)}\approx1+2k\tau\,\dfrac{D}{uL}$
$\dfrac{C}{C_0}=\exp\!\left[-k\tau+(k\tau)^2\dfrac{D}{uL}\right]$
Eq. 20; holds for any Gaussian RTD with $\sigma_\theta^2=2D/uL$
$\dfrac{L}{L_p}=\dfrac{V}{V_p}=1+k\tau\,\dfrac{D}{uL}$
extra size for the same exit concentration
$\dfrac{C}{C_p}=1+(k\tau)^2\dfrac{D}{uL}$
more A left for the same size

Subscript $p$: the plug-flow reactor, $C_p/C_0=e^{-k\tau}$.

BALANCE ON A SLICE, WITH UNITS

$$D\frac{d^2C_A}{dl^2}-u\frac{dC_A}{dl}-kC_A^2=0$$ $$l=0:\ uC_{A0}=uC_A-D\frac{dC_A}{dl}\qquad l=L:\ \frac{dC_A}{dl}=0$$

13.2 · problem statement · read first

Conversion in a reactor that deviates from plug flow

The reactor of Example 13.1 is a tube. Liquid phase $\text{A}+\text{B}\to\text{C}+\text{D}$, $r_1=kC_A$, $k=0.307\ \text{min}^{-1}$; $v=200$ L/min, $V=3\ \text{m}^3=3000$ L, $F_{A0}=200$ mol/min, so $C_{A0}=1$ mol/L and $\bar t=15$ min. Inlet superficial velocity $u=0.1$ m/s.

A pulse-tracer test gave the E curve in the table. Assume the dispersion model represents the flow, with closed ends. Find $D/uL$, the conversion of A, and the tube diameter, length and $D$. Compare with Example 13.1.

$t$ (min)$\mathbf E$ (min$^{-1}$)$t$ (min)$\mathbf E$ (min$^{-1}$)
00200.04
50.03250.02
100.05300.01
150.05350

Same vessel and data as Lecture 12, Example 1.

13.2 · solution, step 1 · from Lecture 12

$\sigma_\theta^2=0.211$, closed vessel: $D/uL=0.120$

Lecture 12$\sigma_\theta^2=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{\bar t^{\,2}},\qquad \sigma_{\theta,cc}^2=2\dfrac{D}{uL}-2\Big(\dfrac{D}{uL}\Big)^2\big[1-e^{-uL/D}\big]$
$$\bar t=\sum t\,\mathbf E\,\Delta t=15\ \text{min}\qquad \sigma^2=\sum t^2\mathbf E\,\Delta t-\bar t^{\,2}=47.5\ \text{min}^2\qquad \sigma_\theta^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{\bar t^{\,2}}=0.211$$
moments of the E curve, $\Delta t=5$ min
$$0.211=2\frac{D}{uL}-2\Big(\frac{D}{uL}\Big)^2\Big[1-e^{-uL/D}\Big]\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{D}{uL}=0.1199$$
closed–closed variance; above 0.01, so not the Gaussian
0.211=2*x-2*(x^2)*(1-EXP(-1/x)) // EQUATRAN: x = D/uL = 0.1199

13.2 · solution, step 2 · Wehner–Wilhelm

Dispersion: $X_A=0.966$, between plug 0.990 and mixed 0.821

Wehner–Wilhelm, first order$\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\dfrac{4a\,e^{uL/2D}}{(1+a)^2e^{a\,uL/2D}-(1-a)^2e^{-a\,uL/2D}},\quad a=\sqrt{1+4k\tau\,(D/uL)}$
$$a=\sqrt{1+4(4.605)(0.1199)}=1.791\qquad \frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=0.0339\qquad X_A=0.966$$
$k\tau=4.605$ from Example 13.1, $uL/D=8.34$
$$\begin{gathered}\text{small-deviation form: }\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\exp\big[-k\tau+(k\tau)^2D/uL\big]=0.127\\ X_A=1-\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=0.873\quad\text{(not valid here)}\end{gathered}$$
needs $D/uL<0.01$; here 0.12 and $k\tau$ is large

Shoot from the exit: $C_A/C_{A0}=0.0339$, $X_A=0.966$

Lecture 12 fitted $N$ to a tracer curve. Now let the fluid react in each tank.

The 1st tank, the 2nd tank, … the Nth

Each tank’s exit is the next tank’s feed

The model’s real payoff: it works with any kinetics, tank by tank.

Tank $i$ of $N$ · mole balance

First order: one tank step 1 of 2

Mole balance, mixed flow, steady state$F_{A,i-1}-F_{A,i}+r_{A,i}V_i=0$   (in − out + generation = 0)
$$v\,C_{A,i-1}-v\,C_{A,i}=kC_{A,i}V_i$$
$F_A=vC_A$, constant density; $-r_A=kC_A$ at the exit concentration (contents = exit)
$$C_{A,i-1}-C_{A,i}=kC_{A,i}\,\bar t_i\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{C_{A,i}}{C_{A,i-1}}=\frac{1}{1+k\bar t_i}$$
divide by $v$; $\bar t_i=V_i/v$
$F_{A,i},\ C_{A,i}$
molar flow and concentration of A leaving tank $i$; $C_{A0}$: feed
mol/s, mol/m³
$V_i,\ \bar t_i$
volume and mean residence time of one tank
m³, s

Tanks in series · first order

First order: N tanks multiply step 2 of 2

One tank$\dfrac{C_{A,i}}{C_{A,i-1}}=\dfrac{1}{1+k\bar t_i}$
$$\frac{C_{AN}}{C_{A0}}=\frac{C_{A1}}{C_{A0}}\cdot\frac{C_{A2}}{C_{A1}}\cdot\frac{C_{A3}}{C_{A2}}\cdots\frac{C_{AN}}{C_{A,N-1}}$$
each exit feeds the next tank; the middle concentrations cancel
$$\frac{C_{AN}}{C_{A0}}=\frac{1}{(1+k\bar t_i)^N}=\frac{1}{\left(1+\dfrac{k\bar t}{N}\right)^N}$$
$N$ equal factors; equal tanks, $\bar t_i=\bar t/N$

$N\to\infty$: $(1+k\bar t/N)^{-N}\to e^{-k\bar t}$, plug flow. Holds for micro- and macrofluids.

Tanks in series · first order

How many tanks are close enough to plug flow?

$X_A$, $N$ tanks–
$X_A$, plug flow–
exactlarge-$N$ form
$V_N/V_p$––
$C_{A,N}/C_{A,p}$––

The gap to plug flow shrinks like $1/N$, and it grows with $k\bar t$: high conversion needs many tanks.

Large N, first order

Close to plug flow: two penalties

N tanks, first order$\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\Big(1+\dfrac{k\bar t}{N}\Big)^{-N}$
$$\text{same }C_{A,\text{final}}:\quad\frac{V_{N\,\text{tanks}}}{V_p}=1+\frac{k\bar t}{2N}$$
expand the N-tank result to first order in $1/N$, match plug flow’s $e^{-k\bar t}$
$$\text{same }V:\quad\frac{C_{A,N\,\text{tanks}}}{C_{A,p}}=1+\frac{(k\bar t)^2}{2N}$$
$\ln(1+x)\approx x-x^2/2$ with $x=k\bar t/N$

Valid while $k\bar t/N$ is small. At $k\bar t=2$, $N=10$: 1.107 exact against 1.10.

Microfluid, $A\to R$ or $A+B\to R$, $C_{A0}=C_{B0}$

Second order: the tank results nest, not multiply

Mole balance on tank $i$, $-r_A=kC_A^2$$C_{A,i-1}-C_{A,i}=kC_{A,i}^{\,2}\,\tau_i$
$$C_{A1}=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+4C_{A0}k\tau_i}}{2k\tau_i}$$
tank 1: solve the quadratic, take the positive root
$$C_{AN}=\frac{1}{4k\tau_i}\left(-2+2\sqrt{\cdots-1+2\sqrt{-1+2\sqrt{1+4C_{A0}k\tau_i}}}\right)$$
feed $C_{A1}$ into tank 2, and so on: $N$ square roots

Two tanks: $C_{A2}=\frac{1}{4k\tau_i}\big(-2+2\sqrt{-1+2\sqrt{1+4C_{A0}k\tau_i}}\big)$. $\tau_i$: space time of one tank, equal to $\bar t_i$ at constant density; $k$ in m³/(mol·s).

Each bar is one tank’s exit; more, smaller tanks follow the plug-flow curve more closely.

For any other rate law there is no closed form: go tank by tank.

All other kinetics, microfluid

Any kinetics: solve tank after tank

Mole balance on tank $i$$\bar t_i=\dfrac{C_{A,i-1}-C_{A,i}}{-r_{A,i}}$   rate taken at its own exit $C_{A,i}$
$$C_{A,i-1}\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{solve for } C_{A,i}\ }\;C_{A,i}\;\to\;\text{feed of tank } i+1$$
one algebraic equation per tank; tedious by hand, trivial in code or EQUATRAN
$$-r_{A,i}=-\frac{1}{\bar t_i}\big(C_{A,i}-C_{A,i-1}\big)$$
the same balance on the rate plot: a line through $(C_{A,i-1},0)$, slope $-1/\bar t_i$

The line meets the rate curve at $C_{A,i}$; equal tanks give parallel lines.

Lecture 13-2

What section 13-2 settled

  • A microfluid needs a mole balance with a flow model; the RTD only fixes its parameter, $D/uL$ or $N$.
  • Plug flow: $dF_A/dV=-(-r_A)$ becomes $u\,dC_A/dl=-(-r_A)$. For Example 13.1 ($k\tau=4.605$): plug 0.990, mixed 0.821.
  • Dispersion adds $\frac{D}{uL}\frac{d^2C}{dz^2}$ and the closed inlet condition. First order, $D/uL=0.12$: Wehner–Wilhelm gives 0.966; the small-deviation form needs $D/uL<0.01$.
  • Other orders: a second-order boundary-value problem. EQUATRAN shoots from the exit and matches the inlet condition.
  • Tanks in series: tank ratios multiply, $(1+k\bar t/N)^{-N}$, 0.962 for $N=5$; second order nests roots; any kinetics, tank after tank.
  • Same $\bar t$ and $\sigma^2$: dispersion and tanks agree within 0.004.

13-3

Lecture 13-3

Macrofluid: how is the segregation model used?

A · Plug flowB · Mixed flowC · Real vesselsExamples 13.4–13.8

Lecture 13-3

One integral, three kinds of E

  1. A · Plug floweach clump is a batch; $\mathbf E=\delta(t-\tau)$; Example 13.4
  2. B · Mixed floworder by order, $\mathrm{ei}(\alpha)$; Example 13.5
  3. C · Real vesselsE from data, dispersion or tanks; Examples 13.6–13.8

13-2 balanced a microfluid. A macrofluid needs a different idea.

Segregated flow model · macrofluid

Each clump is a little batch reactor with its own stay time

No clump exchanges matter with its neighbours; they mix only after leaving.

Segregation model

The exit mix is an age-weighted average step 1 of 2

$\bar C_A$
mean concentration of A in the mixed exit stream
mol/L
$\big(C_A\big)_{batch}$
A left in a clump that has reacted, as a batch, for time $t$
mol/L
$\mathbf E\,dt$
fraction of the exit stream aged between $t$ and $t+dt$
–
$$\left(\begin{array}{c}\text{mean A}\\\text{in exit}\end{array}\right)=\sum_{\text{all ages}}\left(\begin{array}{c}\text{A left in a}\\\text{clump of age }t\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{c}\text{fraction of exit}\\\text{with age }t\end{array}\right)$$
clumps mix only at the exit: a weighted average

Segregation model

Integral, sum, or conversion: one equation step 2 of 2

$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\mathbf E\,dt$$
the sum of step 1 for a continuous E; divide by $C_{A0}$
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}\cong\sum\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\mathbf E\,\Delta t\qquad \bar X_A=\int_0^\infty X_{A,batch}\,\mathbf E\,dt$$
measured E at discrete times; and $X=1-C/C_0$ because $\int\mathbf E\,dt=1$

Needs only two things: the batch kinetics and the E curve. No flow model.

Batch reactor · single reaction, constant volume

The batch results that go inside the integral

Batch balance$\dfrac{dN_A}{dt}=-(-r_A)V,\qquad -r_A=kC_A^{\,n},\qquad C_A=N_A/V$
order$\big(C_A/C_{A0}\big)_{batch}$integrate $dC_A/dt=-kC_A^{\,n}$ from $C_{A0}$
1st$e^{-kt}$$\ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=kt$
2nd$\dfrac{1}{1+kC_{A0}t}$$1/C_A-1/C_{A0}=kt$
$n$th$\big[1+(n-1)C_{A0}^{\,n-1}kt\big]^{1/(1-n)}$$C_A^{1-n}-C_{A0}^{1-n}=(n-1)kt$

Zero order: $1-kt/C_{A0}$ while $t<C_{A0}/k$; at $t=C_{A0}/k$ all A is used up, so 0 after that.

Plug flow sends every clump out at the same age. Its E is a spike.

RTD for plug flow

The Dirac delta: zero width, unit area

$$\delta(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x\ne0\\ \infty & x=0\end{cases}\qquad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x)\,dx=1$$
definition
$$\mathbf E=\delta(t-\tau)\;\Rightarrow\;\int_0^\infty g(t)\,\mathbf E\,dt=g(\tau)$$
sifting: the spike picks one value of $g$
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\delta(t-\tau)\,dt=\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch,\;t=\tau}$$

With $g$ = batch result: plug flow gives the batch answer at $\tau=V/v$, for any order.

Plug-flow reactor · apparent rate $r_1=kC_A^{\,n}$

Microfluid and macrofluid give the same answer in plug flow

Microfluid: $\dfrac{dF_A}{dV}=-r_1$Macrofluid: $\displaystyle\int\Big(\tfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\delta(t-\tau)dt$
1st order$e^{-k\tau}$$e^{-k\tau}$
2nd order$\dfrac{1}{1+k\tau C_{A0}}$$\dfrac{1}{1+k\tau C_{A0}}$
$n$th order$\big[1+(n-1)C_{A0}^{\,n-1}k\tau\big]^{1/(1-n)}$

Entries are $C_A/C_{A0}$ at the exit.

13.4 · problem statement · read first

A macrofluid in the plug-flow reactor of Example 13.1

Liquid phase $\text{A}+\text{B}\to\text{C}+\text{D}$, apparent rate $r_1=kC_A$, $k=0.307\ \text{min}^{-1}$. Inlet volumetric flow rate $v=200$ L/min, reactor volume $V=3\ \text{m}^3=3000$ L, feed $F_{A0}=200$ mol/min, so $C_{A0}=1$ mol/L and $\bar t=15$ min.

The fluid behaves as a macrofluid in an ideal plug-flow reactor. Find the conversion of A with the segregation model, and compare with Example 13.1(b).

13.4 · solution

$X_A=0.990$: the same as the microfluid

Segregation model and plug-flow E$\dfrac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\mathbf E\,dt,\qquad\mathbf E=\delta(t-\tau)$
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^\infty e^{-kt}\,\delta(t-15)\,dt=e^{-0.307\times15}=0.0100$$
first-order batch result, sifted at $t=\tau=15$ min

$\bar X_A=0.990$, identical to Example 13.1(b).

So which vessels need the question at all?

Where we can relax

Where mixing does not matter

Batch reactor

All elements share one history.

Plug flow

All elements share one stay time, so each is an identical batch.

Segregation only matters once the RTD is broad: mixed flow is the extreme.

Mixed flow · microfluid balance

Mixed flow, microfluid step 1 of 2

$$C_{A0}-C_A=(-r_A)\,\bar t$$
balance on the uniform tank; outlet equals contents
$$\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=1-\frac{(-r_A)\,\bar t}{C_{A0}}$$
divide by $C_{A0}$; $-r_A$ is evaluated at $C_A$ itself

$\bar t=V/v$ s; $-r_A$ in mol/(m³·s). Order $n$ gives $-r_A=kC_A^{\,n}$.

Mixed flow reactor · macrofluid

Mixed flow, macrofluid: the exponential RTD in the segregation integral step 2 of 2

$$\mathbf E\,dt=\frac{v}{V}\,e^{-tv/V}\,dt=\frac{e^{-t/\bar t}}{\bar t}\,dt$$
mixed-flow RTD from Lecture 11, $\bar t=V/v$
$$1-\bar X_A=\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\frac{e^{-t/\bar t}}{\bar t}\,dt$$
segregation model of 13-3 with this E

Only the batch result changes from order to order.

Order 1

First order: the two tanks agree

Segregation model, 13-3$\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{\text{batch}}\mathbf E\,dt$
$$\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^\infty e^{-kt}\,\frac{e^{-t/\bar t}}{\bar t}\,dt=\frac{1}{1+k\bar t}$$
first-order batch decay times the mixed-flow $\mathbf E$
$$\text{microfluid: }\;1-\frac{kC_A\bar t}{C_{A0}}=\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{1}{1+k\bar t}$$
Micro balance with $-r_A=kC_A$; same answer

13.5 · problem statement · read first

A macrofluid in the mixed-flow reactor of Example 13.1

Liquid phase $\text{A}+\text{B}\to\text{C}+\text{D}$, apparent rate $r_1=kC_A$, $k=0.307\ \text{min}^{-1}$. Inlet volumetric flow rate $v=200$ L/min, reactor volume $V=3\ \text{m}^3=3000$ L, feed $F_{A0}=200$ mol/min, so $C_{A0}=1$ mol/L and $\bar t=15$ min.

The fluid behaves as a macrofluid in an ideal mixed-flow reactor. Find the conversion of A with the segregation model, and compare with Example 13.1(a).

13.5 · solution

$\bar X_A=0.821$: first order does not see segregation

Segregation model, mixed-flow E$\dfrac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\frac{e^{-t/\bar t}}{\bar t}\,dt$
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\frac{1}{\bar t}\int_0^\infty e^{-kt}e^{-t/\bar t}dt=\frac{1}{1+k\bar t}=\frac{1}{1+4.605}=0.178$$
first-order batch result $e^{-kt}$; integrate the single exponential

$\bar X_A=0.821$, the microfluid value of Example 13.1(a).

Order 0

Zero order: the macrofluid is worse

Batch, zero order$\Big(\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{\text{batch}}=1-\dfrac{kt}{C_{A0}}$ for $t<C_{A0}/k$; $=0$ after (A used up)
$$\text{micro: }\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=1-R\qquad\text{macro: }\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=1-R\big(1-e^{-1/R}\big)$$
Micro balance, and the segregation integral with the cut-off at $t=C_{A0}/k$

$R=k\bar t/C_{A0}$, dimensionless. Macrofluid leaves more A, because clumps that finish early cannot go below zero.

Order 2

Second order: the macrofluid is better

$R$
reaction speed, $C_{A0}k\bar t$
–
$\alpha$
inverse speed, $1/R$
–
$$\text{micro: }\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+4R}}{2R}\qquad\text{macro: }\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\alpha e^{\alpha}\!\int_\alpha^\infty\!\frac{e^{-x}}{x}dx$$
micro: quadratic from the balance; macro: the segregation integral with $1/(1+C_{A0}kt)$

At $R=1$: micro $0.618$, macro $0.596$ left; $X_A=0.382$ against $0.404$.

Second order, macrofluid · the integral

$\mathrm{ei}(\alpha)$: a tabulated function, like $\ln$ or $\exp$

$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\frac{1}{\bar t}\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-t/\bar t}}{1+C_{A0}kt}dt=\alpha e^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{ei}(\alpha)$$
substitute $\theta=t/\bar t$, then $x=\alpha+\theta$
$$\alpha=\frac{1}{C_{A0}k\bar t},\qquad\mathrm{ei}(\alpha)=\int_\alpha^\infty\frac{e^{-x}}{x}dx$$
definition of the exponential integral

Series: $\mathrm{ei}(x)=-0.57721-\ln x+x-\dfrac{x^2}{2\cdot2!}+\dots$

The real vessel has more short-lived fluid than the model

  • Apart from its long tail, the model curve is more bunched around $\bar t$.

Tanks in series · from Lecture 12

The N-tank RTD: one exponential, convolved N times

$$\mathbf E_1=\frac{1}{\bar t_i}e^{-t/\bar t_i}$$
one tank of $N$, $\bar t_i=\bar t/N$: the mixed-flow RTD
$$\mathbf E_2=\int_0^t\mathbf E_1(t')\,\mathbf E_1(t-t')\,dt'=\frac{t}{\bar t_i^{\,2}}e^{-t/\bar t_i}$$
tank 2 is fed by tank 1’s exit: convolution
$$\mathbf E=\frac{t^{N-1}}{(N-1)!\,\bar t_i^{\,N}}e^{-t/\bar t_i}=\frac{N^N\,t^{N-1}}{(N-1)!\,\bar t^{\,N}}e^{-tN/\bar t}$$
repeat $N$ times; put $\bar t_i=\bar t/N$

Dimensionless: $\mathbf E_\theta=\bar t\,\mathbf E=\dfrac{N(N\theta)^{N-1}}{(N-1)!}e^{-N\theta}$, $\theta=t/\bar t$.

$N=1$: mixed flow; $N\to\infty$: a spike at $\theta=1$, plug flow.

segregation integral with the N-tank $\mathbf E$ of the previous slide

13.7 · problem statement · read first

Macrofluid with the tanks-in-series RTD

Liquid phase $\text{A}+\text{B}\to\text{C}+\text{D}$, $r_1=kC_A$, $k=0.307\ \text{min}^{-1}$; $v=200$ L/min, $V=3000$ L, $F_{A0}=200$ mol/min ($C_{A0}=1$ mol/L, $\bar t=15$ min).

The RTD is represented by $N=5$ tanks in series (Example 13.3). Find the conversion of a macrofluid with the segregation model.

13.7 · solution

$\bar X_A=0.962$: again the microfluid value

N-tank RTD, Lecture 12$\bar t\,\mathbf E=\Big(\dfrac{t}{\bar t}\Big)^{N-1}\dfrac{N^N}{(N-1)!}e^{-tN/\bar t}$
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^\infty e^{-kt}\,\frac{1}{\bar t}\Big(\frac{t}{\bar t}\Big)^4\frac{5^5}{4!}e^{-5t/\bar t}dt=1.715\times10^{-4}\int_0^\infty e^{-0.6403t}\,t^4\,dt$$
$N=5$, $\bar t=15$: $5^5/(4!\,15^5)=1.715\times10^{-4}$; $k+N/\bar t=0.6403$
$$\int_0^\infty t^4e^{-at}dt=\frac{4!}{a^5}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=0.0382,\quad\bar X_A=0.962$$
gamma integral; equals the N-tank result exactly

13.8 · problem statement · read first

Macrofluid: noncoalescing droplets in a contactor

Dispersed noncoalescing droplets ($C_{A0}=2$ mol/L) react ($\text{A}\to\text{R}$, $-r_A=kC_A^2$, $k=0.5$ L/mol·min) as they pass through a contactor.

Find the average concentration of A remaining in the droplets leaving the contactor if their RTD is given by the curve.

13.8 · solution

$\bar C_A=0.462$ mol/L, $\bar X_A=0.769$

Segregation model, second-order batch$\dfrac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\mathbf E\,dt,\qquad\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}=\frac{1}{1+kC_{A0}t}$
$$\text{area}=2\times(5-2)=6\;\Rightarrow\;\mathbf E=\tfrac{1}{3}\ \text{min}^{-1}\ \text{for}\ 2\le t\le5,\qquad kC_{A0}=0.5\times2=1\ \text{min}^{-1}$$
normalise the curve; batch group for second order
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_2^5\frac{1}{1+t}\cdot\frac13\,dt=\frac13\ln\frac{6}{3}=0.231\qquad\bar C_A=0.462\ \text{mol/L}$$
segregation model; the droplets’ ages run from 2 to 5 min

The source integrates from 0 to 3 and gets 0.457, $X_A=0.543$. The ages are 2–5 min, so $\bar C_A/C_{A0}=0.231$.

Lecture 13-3

What section 13-3 settled

  • A macrofluid clump is a batch reactor: $\bar C_A/C_{A0}=\int_0^\infty(C_A/C_{A0})_{batch}\mathbf E\,dt$; with data, a sum over $\mathbf E\,\Delta t$.
  • Plug flow: $\mathbf E$ is a Dirac spike, so macro equals micro for any order (Example 13.4, 0.990).
  • Mixed flow: first order gives the same 0.821 (Example 13.5); a macrofluid converts more for $n>1$ (via $\mathrm{ei}(\alpha)$ at second order) and less for $n<1$.
  • Real vessel, first order: measured $\mathbf E$ 0.953 (Example 13.6); dispersion 0.966; tanks, $N=5$, 0.962 (Example 13.7). Same $\sigma^2$, but the models carry less young fluid, so they over-predict.
  • Macrofluid equations matter for solids, bubbles and droplets: Example 13.8, $\bar X_A=0.769$.

A common question from the table: the ideal mixed reactor converts less than the real vessel.

Frequently asked · first order, $k\bar t=4.605$

“Ideal” is a mixing limit, not a performance target

Q. Mixed flow is ideal yet gives 0.821, and the real vessel 0.96. So do we want non-ideal flow?
  • A. No. The real vessel here is a tube; compare it with its own ideal, plug flow: 0.966 < 0.990.
  • For $n>0$, mixed flow runs everywhere at the exit concentration, the lowest rate: it is the worst contactor, chosen for other reasons (temperature control, selectivity, slurries, $n<0$).
  • Less back-mixing raises $X_A$; get it by design (staging, baffles), not by hoping the tank mixes badly.

How much the mixing details matter depends on the RTD’s width

  • Segregation plays no role in plug flow.

  • RTD approaching the exponential of mixed flow: both become increasingly important.
  • Batch reactor: every clump has the same history, so segregation never matters.

First order: plug → mixed equals mixed → plug

$$\text{plug}\to\text{mixed: }\frac{C_{A1}}{C_{A0}}=e^{-k\bar t_p},\quad\frac{C_{A2}}{C_{A1}}=\frac{1}{1+k\bar t_m}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{C_{A2}}{C_{A0}}=\frac{e^{-k\bar t_p}}{1+k\bar t_m}$$
each unit’s first-order ratio, multiplied

multiplication commutes; the ratio ignores the inlet level

13.9 · solution, step 4 · macrofluid, either order

Macrofluid: $\bar X_A=0.799$

Segregation model, 13-3$\dfrac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{batch}\mathbf E\,dt$
$$\mathbf E=0\ \ (t<\bar t_p),\qquad \mathbf E=\frac{1}{\bar t_m}e^{-(t-\bar t_p)/\bar t_m}\ \ (t\ge\bar t_p)$$
the tube delays every element by exactly $\bar t_p=7.5$ min; the tank then adds its exponential RTD, mean $\bar t_m=7.5$ min
$$\frac{\bar C_A}{C_{A0}}=\int_0^{7.5}(\dots)\,0\,dt+\int_{7.5}^\infty\frac{1}{1+0.307t}\cdot\frac{1}{7.5}e^{1-t/7.5}\,dt=0.2011$$
no fluid leaves before 7.5 min; second-order batch $1/(1+kC_{A0}t)$

$\bar X_A=0.799$ — numerically, or as $\alpha e^\alpha\,\mathrm{ei}(\alpha)$ with a shifted origin.

7.5 min is the first exit time, not the mean: $\bar t=\bar t_p+\bar t_m=15$ min. Swapping tube and tank gives the same E.

For $n>1$ late mixing and segregation win; for $n<1$ early mixing wins; at $n=1$ all three coincide.

A tracer test cannot tell these four apart.

Same tracer curve, different insides

One exponential RTD, four patterns

  • (a) mixed flow: the feed blends at once with all the old fluid in the tank.
  • (b) side-feeding plug flow: each side stream lands in fluid that has already travelled part of the tube, so new and old fluid mix the moment they meet: earliest.
  • (c) parallel plug flows: each tube keeps its own age; the streams meet only at the common exit.
  • (d) side-leaving plug flow: fluid leaves at different points and meets only in the exit line: latest.

tracer test on four patterns

Same exit curve, different conversion

$X_A$ microfluid, early–
$X_A$ macrofluid, late–
this pattern–

The exit curve is identical in all four, yet the conversion readouts split into an early-mixing and a late-mixing value.

Bounds

Two bounds for any RTD

Latest-mixing bound = segregation model of 13-3$\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{\text{batch}}\mathbf E\,dt$

Latest mixing

Elements of different age meet only at the exit, so each one reacts as a batch until then: that is the segregation integral, for a macrofluid or a microfluid.

Earliest mixing

Microfluid with the greatest mixedness, found with Zwietering’s method.

Which way does it go?

Which bound gives more conversion?

OrderHigher conversionWhy
$n>1$late mixing, macrofluidrich clumps react fast
$n=1$neitherrate is linear
$n<1$early mixingdilution costs less

A second-order reaction occurs in a reactor whose RTD is given in the figure. Calculate the conversion for the flow schemes shown in this figure. For simplicity take $C_0=1$, $k=1$, and $\tau=1$ for each unit.

Microfluid, schemes (a) and (b)

Second-order unit balances, inlet $C_{in}$$\text{mixed: }k\tau C^2+C-C_{in}=0\qquad\text{plug: }\dfrac{1}{C}=\dfrac{1}{C_{in}}+k\tau$
$$\text{(a) mixed: }C_1=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+4k\tau C_0}}{2k\tau}=0.618\quad\text{plug: }\frac{1}{C_2}=\frac{1}{C_1}+k\tau\Rightarrow C_2=0.382$$

All concentrations in mol/L. Later mixing in (b) leaves less A.

13.10 · step 3 of 4

Latest mixing, schemes (c), (d), (e)

Segregation model, 13-3$\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Big(\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}}\Big)_{\text{batch}}\mathbf E\,dt$

the tube ($\tau=1$) delays every element by 1; the tank ($\tau=1$) then gives $e^{-(t-1)}$

13.10 · step 4 of 4 · Summary of Findings, item 4

Why the answers are so close

Low conversion

RTD, earliness and segregation all hardly matter.

Intermediate

The RTD starts to matter; the other two still hardly do.

High conversion

All three can play a major role.

Example 13.10 sits in the middle band: $X_A$ about $0.62$ to $0.64$.

Effect of kinetics, conversion level and product distribution

When segregation and earliness of mixing matter

Reaction order

$n>1$: late mixing and macrofluid win. $n<1$: reversed. $n=1$: no effect.

Conversion level

Low: nothing matters. Middle: the RTD matters. High: all three may.

Product distribution

Multiple reactions: these factors can dominate even at low conversion.

Lecture 13-4

What section 13-4 settled

  • First order, or plug flow: segregation and earliness change nothing; the RTD alone fixes $X_A$.
  • Other orders: $n>1$ favours segregation and late mixing, $n<1$ the reverse. A broad RTD widens the gap; more tanks close it.
  • Example 13.9, second order, one RTD: mixed→plug (early) 0.773, plug→mixed (late) 0.794, macrofluid 0.799.
  • Any RTD has two bounds: earliest mixing (microfluid) and latest mixing (segregation integral). Example 13.10: five schemes, $X_A$ 0.618 to 0.639.
  • The effects grow with conversion; with multiple reactions they can decide the product distribution even at low conversion.

A and B enter a stirred tank in separate streams

  • Microfluid: free molecules; A meets B and reacts.
  • Macrofluid: only clumps meet; no reaction.
A fed–
R formed–
A reacted–
clumps–

Same tank, same feeds: only molecular contact makes R; clumps that never dissolve pass through unreacted.

Partial segregation

Real fluids lie between

  • Clumps stretch and thin, so A-rich and B-rich regions persist.
  • Reaction happens where the regions touch.

lattice lab

Blue A and orange B in clumps of different size

Each square is a small volume: A, B, R, S, white = used up. Each sweep, neighbours swap places (mixing); an A next to a B reacts with the chance set above.

A left–
R now–
R peak–
S–
sweeps–

Try Clump 2, then Clump 8, and compare A left after the same sweeps: big clumps react only at their edges. ‘Macro’ never swaps, so only the first edges ever react.

Product distribution

Consecutive reactions

Reactions$A+B\xrightarrow{k_1}R\qquad R+B\xrightarrow{k_2}S$
$R$
the wanted intermediate product
–
$S$
unwanted, made where $R$ meets more $B$
–
$\rho$
speed ratio, $k_2/k_1$
–

A | B interface

The reaction zone

  • Fast: a thin zone where $A$, $B$ and $R$ overlap.
  • Infinitely fast: the zone is a plane, and $R$ is trapped against $B$.

Setting up the next lab

How thick is the zone?

$L$
thickness of one A or B stripe
cm
$Da$
reaction speed over diffusion, $k_1C_0L^2/\mathcal D$
–
$$\frac{\text{zone width}}{L}\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{Da}}$$
reactants meet only as far as diffusion reaches during the reaction time

$Da=100$: the zone is a tenth of a stripe. $Da=10^4$: one percent.

reaction-zone lab

Stripes of A and B diffuse and react

Left half starts as A, right half as B. They diffuse toward each other and react where they meet. Large $Da$: fast reaction, thin zone, and the R made there meets more B and becomes S.

zone width–
R made, per A fed–
R if well mixed–
A left–
S–
time–

Raise $Da$ and the zone thins; the wanted R falls from about $0.36$ toward $0.05$ per mole of A.

Random-walk argument

Why R is lost on a plane

$$P_{\text{not yet in B}}(n)\approx\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}}$$
random walk in one dimension, $n$ steps (Feller)
  • An R molecule on the plane steps left or right at random.
  • It almost surely drifts into B-rich fluid, where it becomes $S$.

$n$: number of random steps taken, dimensionless.

random walk

How long does R stay out of the B zone?

simulated–
$\sqrt{2/\pi n}$–

After 1000 steps still about 2.5 % have escaped the B zone: the decay is slow, but the walk always ends.

How a stirred tank really mixes

Feeds are stretched and folded

  • The impeller stretches and folds A and B clumps into thin layers.
  • Thin layers let diffusion finish the mixing.

fold the stripes

Each fold halves the stripe; diffusion time falls fourfold

stripe–
diffusion time–

From a 1 mm stripe, ten folds make a 1 µm stripe and cut the diffusion time from about 1000 s to 1 ms ($\mathcal D=10^{-5}$ cm²/s).

Design consequences

Three rules for the designer

(a) Mix hard

Fold fast so stripes thin before the reaction finishes.

(b) Disperse B in A

Feed B as fine streams into the A-rich fluid.

(c) Slow the reaction

Lower $k$ or concentration so diffusion keeps up.

Lecture 13-5

What section 13-5 settled

  • Where A first meets B can take conversion from its plug-flow value to zero.
  • Microfluid reacts molecule to molecule; real fluids form A-rich and B-rich regions.
  • The zone width is about $L/\sqrt{Da}$; as $Da$ grows it becomes a plane.
  • On a plane, R is lost to B: product distribution can change even at low conversion.
  • Mix hard, disperse B finely in A, or slow the reaction.

Problem I (Part A Problem I of Final Exam 2024) · 1 of 2 · read it all before we start

Mixed flow reactor: aspirin in a 5000 L stirred tank

A 5000 L industrial stirred-tank reactor is used to produce aspirin through the following main reaction. A side reaction also occurs between salicylic acid (SA) and acetic acid (HA).

Recently, reaction kinetics were re-evaluated using a 10 L stirred-tank reactor. The apparent rate law was found to change from first-order (previous result) to third-order kinetics, described by the following rate law: $r_{app}=kC_{SA}^{3}$, $k=5.87\ \text{L}^6/(\text{mol}^2\cdot\text{min})$. This reaction rate law is now applied to estimate the residence time in an industrial-scale 5000 L reactor.

To validate the non-ideal flow behavior in the 5000 L reactor, the effect of rotational speed on performance was investigated. The reactor is designed for continuous flow operation. A series of tracer experiments was conducted at two different agitator speeds, 120 rpm and 180 rpm, as summarized in the table on the next slide.

The liquid feed stream matches the reactant feed, with a flow rate of 125 L/min, and the initial and feed concentrations of salicylic acid are controlled at 1 mol/L.

Problem I · sub-question 2 · ideal CSTR

Ideal CSTR, third order: $X_{SA}=0.847$

Mixed flow, CSTR (continuous stirred-tank reactor)$\tau=\dfrac{V}{v},\qquad C_{SA0}-C_{SA}=(-r)\,\tau,\qquad -r=kC_{SA}^{\,3}$
$$C_{SA0}X=kC_{SA0}^{\,3}(1-X)^3\tau\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{X}{(1-X)^3}=k\tau C_{SA0}^{\,2}$$
put $C_{SA}=C_{SA0}(1-X)$, divide by $C_{SA0}$: two powers of $C_{SA0}$ stay, $n-1=2$
$$\tau=\frac{5000}{125}=40\ \text{min},\quad k\tau C_{SA0}^{\,2}=5.87\times40\times1^2=234.8\;\Rightarrow\;X_{SA}=0.847$$
space time, then solve $X/(1-X)^3=234.8$ by trial

For comparison, an ideal PFR: $C/C_0=(1+2k\tau C_0^2)^{-1/2}=0.046$, $X=0.954$.

Problem II (Part A Problem 1 of Final Exam 2023) · 1 of 2 · read it all before we start

Fixed-bed tube: o-xylene to phthalic anhydride

Partial oxidation of o-xylene in air for the phthalic anhydride production process follows the reaction shown. These strongly exothermic processes are carried out in multitubular reactors cooled by molten salt circulating around the tubes, which exchanges heat to an internal or external boiler.

Reactor dimension. The tubes are 3 m long with an internal diameter of 2.54 cm. The reactor operates isothermally at 350 °C.

Catalyst. V₂O₅ on promoted silica gel, effective spherical diameter 5 mm, particle density 1,300 kg/m³, bed void fraction 0.43.

Feed. Nearly atmospheric (1 bar). Partial pressures: N₂ 0.772 bar, O₂ 0.21 bar, o-xylene 0.018 bar, kept below 1 mol% to stay under the explosion limit. Superficial gas velocity 0.30 m/s; 2500 tubes give 1650 tons/yr.

Kinetics at 350 °C: $r_{app}=k_1P_{xylene}$, $k_1=0.23\ \text{mol}/(\text{s}\cdot\text{m}^3_{bed}\cdot\text{bar})$.

Fluid properties. Diffusivity of xylene in the catalyst pore 5×10⁻⁵ m²/s; gas viscosity 0.01 cP; gas density 0.57 kg/m³. Hint: bed density = (1 − void) × particle density.

Plug flow: $\bar t=10$ s and $X_{xylene}=0.112$

$$X=1-e^{-k\bar t}=1-e^{-0.119}=0.112$$
first-order plug flow

Problem III · sub-question 6 · discussion

Why run it well mixed, if the real tank converts more?

  • At 120 rpm the tank behaves like two tanks: a narrower RTD, so first-order conversion rises above the CSTR’s 0.903.
  • But a side reaction between SA and HA runs in parallel: with multiple reactions, segregation and earliness of mixing can dominate the product distribution, even when $X$ looks fine (13-4).
  • A well-mixed tank also gives uniform temperature and a predictable, scalable design.
Design for the selectivity you can control, not for a conversion the agitator gives by accident.

Problem V · sub-question 6 · recover the design

Two ways back to the design conversion, and one trap

Raise the rate

Higher temperature or higher feed concentration raise $kC_{A0}$.

Raise the residence time

Lower the feed rate, or reduce dead and bypass volume.

The trap

Faster flow lowers $D/uL$ but also lowers $\bar t$: conversion can fall.

Exam criterion: two methods, with the effect on $\bar t$ stated.

Lecture 13

Key Takeaways

1

Non-ideal flow enters at the pilot and plant scale; the RTD measures it, but one RTD can hide different mixing inside.

2

Decide micro or macro first: compare the reaction time with the micromixing time.

3

Microfluid: mole balance with a flow model — plug, $D/uL$, $N$ tanks or mixed; other orders numerically.

4

Macrofluid: average the batch result over $\mathbf E$: $\bar C_A/C_{A0}=\int(C_A/C_{A0})_{batch}\mathbf E\,dt$.

5

The RTD alone is enough only for first order or plug flow; otherwise late mixing helps when $n>1$, hurts when $n<1$.

6

Judge a real reactor against the ideal it was designed as; non-ideal flow is a defect, not a goal.
